stories.title: Badenoch says Tories would scrap inheritance tax on family homes
stories.summary: Tory leader says her party is "coming back", as she aims to convince voters it has changed after 2024 election defeat.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Watch: The big test facing Kemi Badenoch after her conference speech

Published 7 October 2026

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has pledged to scrap inheritance tax (IHT) on family homes while also allowing couples to leave £1m tax-free, in her keynote speech at the party's conference in Birmingham.

Badenoch added her ambition would be for a Conservative government to abolish IHT "as soon as we can afford it", but said she could not currently propose this due to spending commitments on defence, prisons and the economy.

Badenoch also used her speech to try to make clear how the Tories differed to Labour and Reform UK.

She pitched them as the "no-nonsense party" compared to the Reform UK "circus" and accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of wanting to "live in the past".

Tories united behind Badenoch - but party still needs to win over voters Published 23 hours ago

Why Tories are talking about winning the next election Published 1 day ago

What's in the Conservatives' inheritance tax plan and who benefits? Published 23 hours ago

Rival parties hit back and said the proposals for IHT, which is levied on the value of someone's estate when they die, would prioritise support for wealthier people in the country.

Badenoch arrived in Birmingham's Symphony Hall with a message to Conservative Party members that they face a "battle for the soul of the this nation".

She argued her party is "renewed" and "coming back" as she continued efforts to convince voters that it has changed following an historic defeat at the 2024 general election.

In a nod to those who have defected to Nigel Farage's party, Badenoch said: "The Conservatives have had an export boom of drama queens going to Reform.

"This party is now the no drama party, we are the no-nonsense party."

With the party trailing Labour and Reform in the polls, Badenoch acknowledged that people are "looking through the shop window", they "like what they see" but "not enough of them are buying yet, we need to fix that".

Her inspiration for how to revive a long-standing brand was Marks and Spencer (M&S), saying they have "adapted their style for today's market and people are flooding back".

Badenoch added: "Just like M&S, we must learn from our mistakes, win back trust and make people feel good about our party again."

One of the biggest responses in the room from members came as Badenoch made clear she did not want to do an election deal with Reform.

She described many Reform voters as "our people", adding: "We let them down and we want them to come back home."

Following a section of the speech mocking some of Reform's senior figures, Badenoch said: "To those who say 'unite the right', we are not uniting with that.

"People deserve better than that and we are going to give them better than that. Character, conduct, and standards matter."

She also said she did not want to live in a country run by people who "debate whether my mixed-race children are English".

In one of many jibes aimed at Burnham, Badenoch labelled him a "Paddington Bear prime minister" who was "hoping that the problems will just go away".

In the days ahead of Wednesday's speech, there was widespread speculation that Badenoch would announce changes to IHT.

As the opposition leader neared the end of her 66-minute speech, she said IHT was "supposed to be a tax on the super wealthy" but it is "now a tax on ordinary middle-class families in every corner of our country".

She said: "The next Conservative government will legislate so nobody will ever pay inheritance tax on their family home.

"On top of that, couples would be able to leave an additional £1m tax-free and these changes mean every inheritance tax bill will be cut and the number of families paying inheritance tax will fall by more than half."

The Conservatives have estimated the policy would cost around £6bn a year and believe they have identified £71bn of savings that can be made to government spending, including welfare cuts.

Under the current rules, estates worth more than £325,000, or £500,000 if a home is left to children or grandchildren, can face a 40% tax rate on assets above the threshold.

Married or civil partners can also transfer assets between each other.

In 2023-24, 4.72% of UK deaths resulted in an IHT charge and raised around £7bn for the government.

Badenoch also said her "ambition is to abolish inheritance tax altogether, as soon as we can afford it".

Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "The Tories haven't changed.

"Kemi Badenoch has shown that the Tories' choice is to do nothing to help ordinary families struggling with the cost of social care, prioritising the wealthiest instead."

Reform UK economy spokesman Robert Jenrick said Badenoch had "chickened out of doing anything big" and is "for the 2%".

The former Tory MP said: "While the Tory Party is offering handouts to multi-millionaires, Reform will give everyone a £500 tax cut by raising the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000.

"The Tory Party is looking after its own in Kensington, Reform is looking after the country."

Kemi Badenoch with her husband, Hamish Badenoch, leaving the stage after delivering her keynote speech

Elsewhere in her speech, Badenoch referred to other policies the party has announced in recent days.

These include a £10bn anti-missile defence system , 50,000 new prison places and halving the rate of employer national insurance on earnings for people aged between 21 to 24.

They also pledged to scrap the "cliff edge" that means parents in England lose out on childcare support when they earn more than £100,000 a year.

Another policy to be scrapped would be the High Value Council Tax Surcharge (HVCTS), dubbed the "mansion tax".

This is due to take effect from 2028 and introduces an extra levy for owners of properties in England valued at more than £2m.

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey responded to the speech by saying Badenoch had been "lecturing the country on fiscal responsibility while making tens of billions in unfunded promises".

Green MP Carla Denyer added: "Kemi Badenoch once again defined the Conservative Party as pro-billionaires, pro-inequality and pro-damaging the environment."

stories.body:
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage (right) and Dan Jukes both feature in the undercover filming

Published 7 October 2026

An internal investigation by Reform UK has said the party did not breach electoral law when senior officials were recorded by an undercover journalist discussing a potential way to secure foreign donations to the party.

Reform leader Nigel Farage's senior aide Dan Jukes and the party's head of policy James Orr both stood down pending the outcome of the inquiry.

The investigation concluded that neither of the men did anything that constitutes a breach of the law.

The Metropolitan Police is carrying out a separate criminal investigation into Reform UK , over allegations it broke foreign funding laws.

It came after undercover filming, carried out by Verbatim Investigations and broadcast by Channel 4 News, showed the two aides apparently suggesting a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations, one of which would have totalled £500,000.

The BBC has been told Reform UK will wait until the conclusion of the police investigation before deciding the futures of Jukes and Orr.

In the Channel 4 News report, an undercover investigator posing as the son of an American donor is recorded raising a concern that his father would not be able to directly donate to the party within the law.

Electoral law states that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.

Jukes appears to suggest that the donation could be in the UK-based son's name, although the money would have come from his American father.

Elsewhere, Orr suggests that the father could pay for opinion polling to support one of Reform's campaigns.

Channel 4 News says Reform commissioned three polls costing £32,500 in total and that the public was not told who commissioned or funded them. Reform says it did not commission or pay for the polls.

The party's investigation says invoices for the polling were sent to and paid for by a US company, which was set up by Verbatim.

Farage and Jukes were also filmed at a lunch in Clacton where it is suggested the US donor, who was being played by an actor, gives £500,000 to Reform through his son.

Farage previously told the BBC he "frankly wasn't listening" to the discussion about the potential donation.

Why Reform UK undercover donations claims are legally complicated Published 5 September

Reform UK winded by donations row as insiders call for shift in approach Published 5 September

Reform's investigation concluded no donation was made or accepted by the party and "the party's procedures for checking donors were never reached".

The report says Jukes commissioned the three polls personally, describing him as a "contractor" and not an employee of Reform.

It added there was "no evidence that any individual knowingly took part in an arrangement to facilitate a donation from an impermissible source".

However, it found "people speaking for the party said things that were wrong, careless and in one instance untrue".

The investigation also found "the party's arrangements allowed a sustained deception to reach its leader without anyone asking the questions that would have exposed it".

It added that the party would implement changes to "prevent that from happening again".

Jukes welcomed the findings of the investigation, saying he was "considering all appropriate legal remedies in relation to any false and damaging statements made about me".

He added: "For now, I will continue to take a break from politics to pursue other opportunities."

Reform UK said the internal investigation "found no evidence that any laws were broken".

"Reform UK takes its obligations on governance and conduct extremely seriously," the party said.

"We consider that the production company - Verbatim - acted unlawfully and will be taking the appropriate legal action in due course."

A spokesperson for Verbatim, which was founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting, said: "We are confident in our journalism, which speaks for itself."

A Channel 4 News spokesperson said the broadcaster "stands by its journalism", adding: "The investigation underwent extensive editorial and external legal scrutiny prior to broadcast."

Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson described the internal investigation as a "whitewash", adding: "Nothing in it exonerates Reform or Nigel Farage from the serious allegations that they still face."

stories.summary: Joshua Kerry, 28, appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court and was remanded in custody.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 7 October 2026

The man accused of murdering the former MP Ann Widdecombe in July has appeared in court faced with a new allegation of preparing terrorist acts, including trying to break into the home of Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Prosecutor Kashif Malik said Joshua Kerry, 28, is alleged to have carried out online reconnaissance of "prominent people and institutions... including identifying the home address of Nigel Farage".

The prosecutor later told Westminster Magistrates' Court that damage was found on the doorframe at Farage's home address, adding: "the inference is that an attempt was made to gain entry to the house".

Kerry was accompanied by four custody officers in the dock and was remanded in custody to appear at the Old Bailey on Friday.

Kerry appeared in person the court. With a thick beard and wearing a grey sweatshirt and trousers, he spoke only to confirm his address in Rotherham and his date of birth.

He was told he faced a new charge of preparing terrorist acts between 31 May 2024 and 8 July 2026 by carrying out research on targets and travelling to, and attempting to gain entry to, the home of Nigel Farage.

The court heard that in April 2025 Nigel Farage's partner found that damage had been caused to their main front door at their house and a bottle of lighter fluid was found in the porch.

Kerry was charged in July with the murder of 78-year-old Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman.

Widdecombe was found dead on 9 July at her home in Haytor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries.

She served as Conservative MP for Maidstone and the Weald in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s. She became a member of Reform UK in 2019.

stories.title: Greens face conference centre ban over Zionism motion
stories.summary: Brighton & Hove City Council says the motion is not compatible with its inclusion commitments.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Green Party conference was held in October at the Brighton Centre

Published 7 October 2026

The Green Party of England and Wales could be barred from holding future conferences at the Brighton Centre after the party passed a motion declaring Zionism was racism .

The leader of Brighton & Hove City Council (BHCC), Labour's Bella Sankey, said she was "deeply concerned at the prospect of the Green Party returning to Brighton for future conferences".

She claimed the motion was "divisive, discriminatory and wrong" and was not compatible with Brighton & Hove's commitments to be a welcoming and inclusive city.

Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader, said he would "not accept any exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone, because of the religious or communal body they are part of".

Refusing future bookings

BHCC owns and operates the Brighton Centre, which has hosted party political conferences for decades.

Sankey told the BBC she was considering refusing to allow the Greens to hire the venue for future events.

In a statement, she claimed the motion had "dangerously" conflated the right of Jewish self-determination with the actions of the Israeli government and risked "the safety of Jewish members and Jewish people more broadly".

Sankey said people should never feel excluded due to their religion or beliefs

Zionism is the belief in the right to a Jewish homeland.

Sankey went on to accuse the Green Party's leadership of a "dereliction of duty", adding "the Brighton Centre is owned by all of us in the city and should never be a place where people feel excluded due to their religion or beliefs".

Green Party sources have rejected Sankey's characterisation of the motion.

Polanski, who is Jewish, said that antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state "are, and must always be, completely distinct - blurring the line between the two is not only wrong but antisemitic, and makes Jewish people less safe".

He added: "It's our role as a movement for justice to protect both the rights of Palestinians and our Jewish communities here in the UK."

The Brighton Centre was used by both the Greens and Liberal Democrats to host their autumn conferences this year.

The venue has also hosted Labour's annual gathering in previous years.

In 2017, the council's then-leader, Warren Morgan, who also represented Labour, threatened to ban his own party from holding its conference at the venue , external over concerns that anti-semitic views had been aired.

stories.title: The candidates hoping to be London's second Tory mayor
stories.summary: The Tory party has closed applications to be their candidate for mayor and there are four hopefuls.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
City Hall, the headquarters of the Greater London Authority

Published 7 October 2026

"We need to treat London seriously" - the words of a leading Conservative MP as his party considers its next candidate to be mayor of the capital.

The party has just closed applications for the role and there are four runners who have openly declared.

In 26 years, the Tories have only had one mayor in the capital, Boris Johnson, who won two elections and served from 2008 to 2016.

The party has lost three elections since then to Sadiq Khan, now Lord Khan of Tooting.

Gareth Bacon MP, shadow minister for London, told a meeting at the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham this week that his party had treated the mayoralty like a "paper candidacy" in the past two elections - meaning that they hadn't taken it seriously enough.

Bacon said that the party had "cut Susan Hall adrift", a reference to their candidate in the last mayoral election in 2024, when Lord Khan won that historic third term as mayor.

Bacon went on to describe Lord Khan as "toxic and divisive".

Boris Johnson was the first - and so far only - Tory mayor of London

The election for mayor of London will be held in May 2028.

That is more than 18 months away, but the race is well under way.

Reform UK selected their candidate, Leila Cunningham, in January.

Sarah Olney, MP for Richmond Park, and Rob Blackie, who ran in 2024, are both candidates for the Lib Dem nomination.

This time round, with speculation about whether the current mayor will stand for a fourth term, the Conservatives sniff a chance.

On the back of local elections in May 2026 when the party won back traditional strongholds like Westminster and Wandsworth from Labour, they feel the mood may be changing.

However, winning the mayoralty may be too big a task. Much of it will depend on who they choose as their candidate.

So who's in the running?

Sir James Cleverly MP

Sir James Cleverly served as a government minister under several prime ministers

As the putative front runner, Braintree MP and former home secretary and foreign secretary James Cleverly has been working the conference circuit very hard.

Once a London Assembly member, and former head of the London Fire Authority, he is seen by many Tories as the 'shoo-in' candidate.

But he will come with baggage - he is a Brexiteer and when he was head of London's Fire Authority oversaw a big cuts programme.

He told me: "I hope to be a real champion for London, not just an administrator. I would make sure people are safe on the street and can really make a life for themselves and their families and can afford to live in London."

Cleverly said party political affiliations "are less important than someone with a real plan to make London a city we can be proud of again".

He added: "I hope to get the candidacy and then be a real champion for London, not just an administrator but a real champion and it's the city I love and that's why I want to put myself forward."

Festus Akinbusoye

Festus Akinbusoye is a former Bedfordshire police and crime commissioner

Festus Akinbusoye is a relative newcomer to London politics, though not to the city.

He emigrated from Nigeria with his parents and sister at age 13 in 1991 and lived in Canning Town in east London.

Akinbusoye was the Bedfordshire police and crime commissioner from 2021 to 2024 and was elected to Westminster City Council in May.

He told me: "We do not have to accept that this is the best we can get.

"I believe that we don't have to accept that just because we're a global city, London has got to be so unaffordable to build a life in.

"I want to be the most pro-policing, pro-house building, pro-business, pro-family, pro-growth mayor London has ever had.

"We can make that happen because London works when Londoners work".

Andrew Boff

Andrew Boff has been on the London Assembly since 2008

Andrew Boff is the current chair of the London Assembly.

Privately, Conservatives joke that it wouldn't be a mayoral selection without him in it. He's been an assembly member since 2008.

They also know he thinks very deeply about the capital's issues, particularly housing.

Why put his name forward again?

He told me: "I've got a very ambitious programme of not telling people how much I love London - because I'm hoping all the candidates love London - but specifically what I'm going to do.

"One of the things we've got to do is help the family housing crisis, so I will make sure we get more money for building those important family-sized homes.

"We need more encouragement for young people to do self-building in housing, so I'll be making land available for young people to build their own homes without having to pay for the cost of the land."

Boff added: "I'll get rid of the outward extension of the Ulez."

Alex Challoner

Alex Challoner said he has made his home in London for more than 30 years

Public affairs professional Alex Challoner told me he came to London from the West Country when he was 21 and has called the city his home for 35 years.

He said: "I think as a party, we have a choice between winning and losing for a fourth consecutive time.

"If we're serious about winning we have to have some of the boldest policies that will appeal to Londoners.

"I'm proposing a crackdown on fair dodgers at the Tube barriers by introducing British Transport Police, as well as training up Transport for London staff to stop people breaking through the barriers."

He told me his plan, called Fare Watch, would use a "simple reporting tool in the TfL Go app and online" where passengers will be able to report persistent fare dodging.

Challoner also pledged to introduce "a London Plan that you can read in an afternoon" as well as VAT cut "for gyms and London breweries".

The hopefuls in the race to be the Conservative mayoral candidate will have to wait until November to find out if they've made the final shortlist.

It is believed that London party members will then be offered a choice of two candidates.

I'm told the final two are likely to be announced on 20 November.

The original proposed date had been Friday the 13th, until it was pointed out that that may not be the most auspicious date to unveil candidates.

stories.title: Ex-Welsh Green Party deputy says Zionism motion 'pointless' after quitting party
stories.summary: Phil Davies called for Welsh Greens to set up their own party in the wake of the conference row.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Phil Davies was a youth activist and campaigner when he was chosen to be the Greens' deputy leader in Wales in 2024

Published 7 October 2026

The Green Party's former deputy leader in Wales says he resigned over the motion to declare "Zionism is racism" because it was "pointless" and some of the statements made were "disgraceful".

Phil Davies announced on social media on Tuesday his decision to quit the party had been "accelerated" by Sunday's conference motion.

In the post he had described the motion as "imperialistic" and "idiotic", and said Welsh Greens should consider splitting away from the English part of the party.

In response party leader Zack Polanski reissued a statement, originally sent on Monday , saying he would not accept anyone being excluded from the party "because of the religious or communal body they are part of".

The party leader, who is Jewish, added that "anti-semitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct".

What is Zionism? A very brief history

The motion, which was passed at a party conference to become party policy , called for a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

In response, Israel banned Polanski from entering the country, while Jewish groups described it as an "attack" on their community and some Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs reported the party to Great Britain's equality watchdog.

Speaking to BBC Radio Wales Breakfast on Wednesday, Davies said he did not know why the motion was discussed "as it doesn't do anything to materially improve people's lives in Palestine".

He said Welsh Greens leader Anthony Slaughter had been supportive of his decision to quit, and also said he hoped Welsh party members would vote to split from those in England at a conference next month.

Welsh first minister says Green Party Zionist motion was ill-judged Published 1 day ago

Green member behind Zionism motion named as 'close friend' of jailed al-Qaeda supporter in court Published 1 day ago

Davies said it was "not the sort of politics" he wanted to be associated with, and that Slaughter had been supportive of his decision to leave the party.

He said: "Our views are exactly the same to be honest with you.

"He sent me a very nice message yesterday as well. I class Anthony as a close friend and that will remain."

When asked on whether Slaughter would follow him in quitting the party, Davies said he did not agree with any elected official resigning and staying in the Senedd.

"You weren't voted in as an individual member under this system. You're voted in under your party banner," he added.

He suggested that Welsh members of the party should consider splitting from the Green Party of England and Wales (GPEW) to "stand on our own two feet as a Welsh party" in light of the motion.

Davies said he was "hoping they'll vote to leave" at their party conference next month.

In an Instagram post, Davies said he had not been treated with respect or been "given enough support from the GPEW".

He added: "I have often felt like the token Welshman moaning at various points, but have not seen enough action taken by GPEW.

"I also feel the position of Wales deputy leaders is ignored rather than supported by GPEW."

Slaughter, who revealed he had been diagnosed with cancer last month, said his former colleague had brought a "much needed new perspective to Welsh politics".

He said: "I am positive he will contribute a great deal to Welsh public life whatever his next steps are.

"While the recent motion is not the only reason for Phil's resignation, I know it has stirred emotions across our party as people express their positions on this issue."

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said on Tuesday that the Green Party policy was "ill-judged" , saying that he had always advocated the two-state solution.

He had been responding to Reform Wales leader Helen Jenner, who had accused "left-wing parties" of having a "sickening antisemitism problem".

Speaking in the Senedd on Tuesday, ap Iorwerth said he always advocated the two-state solution and stood "shoulder to shoulder with the Jewish communities in Wales".

stories.title: Bid to run new trains on West Coast Mainline refused
stories.summary: Plans for more trains would “likely increase delays and cancelled trains", the rail regulator says.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The West Coast Main Line is already under significant pressure, Stephanie Tobyn, from the Office of Rail and Road said

Published 8 October 2026, 12:42 BST

Plans for new train services between London and Wrexham, Rochdale and Blackpool have been rejected by the Office of Rail and Road (ORR).

The proposal to add more trains on the West Coast Main Line would "likely increase delays and cancelled trains for passengers", the regulator said.

It rejected an application from Wrexham, Shropshire and Midlands Railway (WSMR) for five daily Wrexham to London Euston return services, as well as Lumo's proposal for up to four return services between Rochdale and Euston on weekdays and Saturdays, and three on Sundays.

Avanti West Coast's plans for additional services between Blackpool and Euston were also denied by the ORR.

The regulator said: "Gaps in the current timetable need to provide important space for trains to recover when disruption occurs, minimising delays to passengers.

"ORR concluded that adding more services into these windows in the timetable for recovery would reduce that resilience, increasing the risk of disruption spreading to other services and affecting more passengers."

'Heavily used'

Stephanie Tobyn, from the ORR, said: "New services, destinations and greater choice can bring real benefits for passengers and communities.

"But the West Coast Main Line is already under significant pressure, with performance reflecting limited resilience on a heavily used part of the rail network.

"Our detailed analysis has shown that adding more trains to the current timetable would reduce the ability to recover when disruption occurs, increasing the risk of delays spreading and making reliability of the network worse for all passengers."

The ORR said its assessment and decision came after similar applications were rejected in 2025.

The plans would have seen five services per day between Wrexham General and London Euston, taking about three hours

A petition , external , calling on the UK government to support the plans for new services between Wrexham and London, was created by Julia Buckley, MP for Shrewsbury, and reached the required 10,000 signatures to be discussed in parliament in June this year.

At the time, the Department for Transport said that, while it acknowledged the "potential connectivity benefits", it was "unable to direct the ORR in its decision making".

Reacting to the ORR's rejection of the proposals, Buckley said she was "deeply disappointed".

"This is a setback, but it is not the end of our campaign.... I will continue to fight," she added.

'Urgent need'

A spokesperson for WSMR said it was "disappointed" by the decision, "especially after the effort we've made to overcome the concerns raised by statutory consultees over the past two-and-a-half years".

"Improving connectivity is a driver of economic growth and productivity, and WSMR would have unlocked much-needed educational, leisure and work opportunities for communities between north Wales, Midlands and London corridor.

"Since our application was submitted in March 2024, we have received overwhelming backing from local people, businesses, councillors and MPs, who all recognise the urgent need for this improved connectivity. We are very grateful for this support."

stories.title: Plans to shut Marston's Brewery in Burton revealed
stories.summary: Burton-upon-Trent's links with beer and brewing date back centuries.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Marston's Brewery, its history and legacy in the town were "iconic", Carlsberg Britvic said

Published 8 October 2026, 15:03 BST

Marston's Brewery could close in Burton-upon-Trent, under plans revealed by its owners.

Carlsberg Britvic said it was proposing to shut the facility together with its primary logistics operation based at that site next summer. About 310 people are affected.

Burton-upon-Trent's connections with the brewing industry date back centuries, with the firm describing its own history and legacy in the town as "iconic".

However, it said the "stark reality" was that UK cask ale volumes had more than halved in less than a decade and "this trend looks set to continue across the UK".

The company said "priority brands" including Hobgoblin, McEwan's and Brooklyn were expected to remain in its portfolio, but it is unclear where they will be brewed.

Other, smaller brands could find a home under specialist or local brewers, the firm said.

Some have described Burton as the "beer capital of England", and at its height more than 30 breweries once operated from there.

The Staffordshire town links with beer date back to the 11th Century when monks first started brewing.

Key decisions

Camra chairman Ash Corbett-Collins, who grew up in Burton, said statements from Carlsberg about understanding the importance of the brewery to the town "come far too little too late for most people".

"This announcement is an absolute disgrace, and the latest in a string of actions that show how little they care about our brewing heritage or the nation's drinkers."

But he agreed "with Carlsberg on one thing", adding the "time is right to think about alternative, independent, brewers who are willing to become custodians of Carlsberg's cask brands".

Carlsberg Britvic said it told colleagues and trade union partners the news earlier on Thursday.

CEO Paul Davies said the proposal was "by no means a reflection on any of our people, and every effort will be made to help them through this period of uncertainty".

He added Marston's Brewery and the primary logistics operation were expected to continue to operate "during the transition period, while the company works through the detail of the consultation".

"As and when key decisions are taken over the coming months, we will share further information with the industry, but always with our colleagues first."

Then prime minister David Cameron gave US president Barak Obama a crate of Hobgoblin at the G20 summit in Toronto in 2010

Davies said it was important to ensure the firm's portfolio was focused "where consumers are today, and where customer demand is growing".

He added: "That said, smaller ale brands are much loved by select consumers, and we will do everything we can to ensure they thrive under more specialist or local ownership in the future."

It is not the first big brewing firm to move operations in the West Midlands.

Banks's Brewery pulled production out of Wolverhampton in 2025, after 150 years, moving it to Burton.

Carlsberg Marston's Brewing Company, which is headquartered in Wolverhampton, had announced in 2024 that the Burton facility would close as part of a company restructuring.

Burton beer is known for its earthy, eggy smell - known in brewing circles as "Burton snatch" - a sure sign of the ale's quality and provenance.

This is created by the water trickling through unusually thick bands of gypsum under the town, before resting in underground aquifers.

stories.title: Chrysler Building to get its crown restored after being sold
stories.summary: The distinctive Manhattan skyscraper will undergo a major renovation and provide a new supply of offices.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The skyscraper was briefly the world's tallest building

Published 2 hours ago

The Chrysler Building, one of the most distinctive high-rises in Manhattan's skyline, will undergo a major renovation as part of a multi-million-dollar sale deal.

The skyscraper, opened in New York nearly 100 years ago, will see its Art Deco crown polished and restored during a refurbishment that will also involve the restoration of the building's 77-storey façade.

Developer Tishman Speyer has taken over the lease from the Cooper Union for the Advancement of Science and Art, a private college.

Tishman Speyer and its partners will invest $235m (£178m) in the project, as part of which it will upgrade the 61st floor, which is home to huge eagle gargoyles and will also feature an "upscale" lounge.

The developer is planning to use most of the building, which is close to Grand Central railway station, for office space. It is following what it calls a "prebuild approach" that will allow firms to move into their new premises quickly.

Tishman Speyer explained that the area "has one of the lowest office availability rates in Manhattan", adding: "Construction of new office supply in the neighbourhood has been virtually nonexistent for decades."

The renovation will include internal work, such as upgrades to the building's mechanical, elevator, electrical and air handling systems.

At 1,046ft (319m), the Chrysler Building was once the world's tallest building - before being usurped less than a year later by the nearby Empire State Building.

Financed by Walter Chrysler, the motor magnate, the skyscraper's construction began in 1928 and was completed two years later.

Architect William Van Alen modelled the eagle gargoyles on hood ornaments found on the 1929 Chrysler car.

Popping out for lunch: a worker eats a sandwich during construction of the Chrysler Building

The Cooper Union college, whose alumni include inventor Thomas Edison, has owned the land on which the Chrysler Building stands since 1902.

The land was bequeathed to it by the children of Peter Cooper, a manufacturer and industrialist who founded the college in 1859.

As part of the deal, Tishman Speyer will make ground lease payments to the Cooper Union which the college wants to use to finance "a bold plan to restore full-tuition scholarships for all undergraduates".

Cooper Union's president Steven McLaughlin, said: "The significance of this agreement is ultimately about what it makes possible for generations of Cooper Union students."

stories.summary: The Martin Group has become one of the UK's biggest car park operators after buying NCP out of administration.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 8 October 2026, 12:48 BST

A Londonderry company has become one of the UK's biggest car park operators after buying NCP out of administration.

The deal means the Martin Group will control more than 100 sites.

The NCP business collapsed in March 2026 after a sustained period of declining performance left it unable to pay its debts.

At that time some of its sites were closed or transferred to other operators.

'A period of uncertainty'

The administrators, PwC, said the majority of NCP's 145 sites would now transfer to the Martin Group along with the staff who work there.

Zelf Hussain, joint administrator and partner at PwC, said the deal protected hundreds of jobs and delivered the best outcome for creditors.

"Keeping NCP's car parks open also helps keep Britain's town and city centres moving," he added.

"We would like to thank all of NCP's staff and directors for their support and professionalism throughout what has understandably been a period of uncertainty."

NCP's major problems included being locked into long-term leases with property owners and building up a large amount of debt.

The Martin Group already has a substantial commercial property portfolio across the UK including the Fishergate Shopping Centre in Preston and the Mercury Shopping Centre in Romford.

It has recently expanded its hotels business, developing The Bedford Hotel in Belfast and buying The Waterfoot in Derry.

'A fantastic day for NCP'

Gary Martin, director of Martin Property Group, said the company's goal was to "build on the strength and heritage of the NCP brand so it can once again deliver the lasting impact on the communities it serves".

"NCP is an iconic brand with a loyal customer base and talented workforce," he added.

Rob England, chief executive of NCP, said it was "a fantastic day for NCP".

"We have had to make difficult, necessary decisions to keep the business moving forward," he said.

England said NCP was "immensely grateful" to its employees, customers and suppliers and its priority was "to restore full operational momentum and build a sustainable platform for long-term growth".

stories.title: Asos hackers took more personal details than first revealed, BBC finds
stories.summary: Retailer issues update after BBC contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond "basic contact details"
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 8 October 2026, 10:29 BST

Asos has told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the online store's users.

It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.

Names, addresses, phone numbers, emails and customer numbers are now in the hands of cyber criminals.

So too are the searches customers have made on the website. Terms like "reclaimed vintage", "glamorous wide fit" and "Asos petite" are visible in the data.

With this information, scammers may be able to craft potent phishing attack emails or phone calls.

The risk to individuals is now higher and customers are being warned about potential impersonation scams.

In its email to customers, Asos confirmed data profiles were taken but said no bank details or passwords were accessed.

"Please remain cautious of unexpected messages or calls claiming to be from Asos," it said.

"We will never ask you to share passwords, security codes or payment details through an unsolicited message or call."

The company did not respond to questions about the scale of the breach.

The high profile hack made global headlines on Tuesday when cyber criminals used Asos's own app system to send a pop up notification to potentially millions of people.

Later that day the firm confirmed to shareholders via the London Stock Exchange that the pop up was sent by an "unauthorised third party" and "basic personal information including name and contact details may have been accessed."

The company then sent an email to customers with similar wording.

On Wednesday evening the cyber criminals responsible contacted the BBC sharing a sample of the stolen data which showed the true extent of the hack.

The BBC held off publishing this article to allow Asos to contact its customers first.

Customers saw this pop up notification on Tuesday

Asos said it is still investigating the data breach and it would "contact customers directly where we believe additional information, support or action may be required".

The UK fashion site explained to customers that hackers gained access to an Asos employee account by "impersonating a trusted contact to obtain log in credentials".

With that log in to an unnamed service, the hackers were able to download the customer data.

In the pop up notification send to customers by the hackers, they claimed they had "compromised the Snowflake instance".

Snowflake is a popular data storage and analysis company whose customers have been breached in the past due to unauthorised log ins.

The cyber criminals, calling themselves Xuanyewen, claimed to the BBC they used a platform which is built natively on top of Snowflake - called Simon AI - to gain access to the data.

Simon AI has been contacted for comment. Snowflake previously said its platform had not been breached.

Asos said customers are not being asked to take any action.

But cyber security experts have warned users to change passwords as a precaution and be on alert for suspicious activity.

"Passwords have not been stolen, so be highly suspicious of any unsolicited text or email asking you to change or share yours," said Trevor Dearing, Senior Director of Critical Infrastructure at Illumio.

"Expect scammers to mention the attack, use your personal details to seem genuine, and create urgency, such as threatening to lock your account within 24 hours."

Asos said its website and app are safe to use and "we know our customers trust us with their information".

"We take that responsibility seriously and have already taken additional steps to further strengthen security controls," it said.

stories.body:
The Tory leader’s proposal to slash the tax would shovel £6bn of taxpayer money to the already-wealthy

Kemi Badenoch’s inheritance tax gambit is a Conservative classic. After all, it was George Osborne’s high-profile pledge to “take the family home out of inheritance tax” in 2007 that put Gordon Brown off calling a snap general election.

In practice, Osborne’s plan involved a £1m threshold for inheritance tax – and given the global financial crisis had blown a hole in the public finances by the time the Conservative-Lib Dem coalition came to power in 2010, it never came to pass.

But the promise was grabby enough to change the political conversation – and contributed to Brown’s fateful decision not to go to the polls early.

So politically, Badenoch’s flagship policy may have merit. IHT, as policymakers call it, is notoriously unpopular. Families never likely to be liable nevertheless fret about their kids having to paying it, while a cacophony of highly paid tax advisers offer to help them avoid it.

The furious response to Rachel Reeves’s reform of the inheritance tax regime for family businesses and farms, with tractors streaming down Whitehall , underlined how unpopular it is.

But whatever its political logic, the Tory plan makes little economic sense. First, it’s worth pausing to underline how very wealthy the beneficiaries of this new policy are likely to be.

The latest data from HMRC shows that less than 5% of estates – the wealthiest 5%, that is – were liable for any inheritance tax at all in 2023/24.

And under current rules, by combining their tax-free allowances, a married couple can already pass on a property worth up to £1m to their children or grandchildren, without them being liable to pay a penny in inheritance tax.

Badenoch’s new, much more generous regime would permit a couple to pass on the entire family home, however valuable, without paying any tax on it at all; and for good measure an additional £1m in other assets. And the more valuable the property, the bigger the gain.

Clearly, in a sluggish economy where resources are stretched, there’s a question about whether that is the best use of the £6bn of taxpayers’ money the policy is reckoned to cost – compared with, say, investing in infrastructure where there might be the prospect of a return.

Total revenue from IHT is forecast to be about £9bn this year, rising to £15bn by 2030-31 – Badenoch’s plan would wipe out about half of that.

Worse than that though, it will create perverse incentives for older homeowners to do exactly what the economy needs them not to do, and hang on in a valuable property, for fear the proceeds of downsizing would be grabbed by HMRC .

after newsletter promotion

The Tories claim they’ll also abolish stamp duty, helping to oil the wheels of the property market and encourage downsizing; but for the most valuable homes, the benefits of not paying 40% inheritance tax above the current threshold would be likely to more than overwhelm the boon of a tax-free move.

And that would be likely to mean far fewer family-size homes coming on to the market in the places up-and-coming buyers most need them to be available.

As Arun Advani, of the Centre for the Analysis of Taxation at the University of Warwick, points out, the biggest beneficiaries would be in areas where housing is expensive.

He says: “‘Where housing is expensive’ mostly means ‘where lots of people want to live’, usually because there are good jobs. Reducing housing sales here will make it harder for young working families trying to upsize. By staying put, they will in turn make it harder for school leavers and university/college graduates to move to the area for work. This is bad for growth,” he said.

Indeed, he points out there would even be an incentive for those who can afford it to “upsize” – moving to a larger house, which would then effectively shelter the asset from inheritance tax.

If Badenoch and her party want to shovel an additional £6bn of taxpayers’ money to the already-wealthy in the hope of winning back votes in the stockbroker belt, so be it – but she should not be able to claim the policy would be anything but bad for economic growth.
